## Overview

The Nandi are a Southern Nilotic tribe of the Kalenjin ethnic group. They historically occupied the highland areas of the former Rift Valley Province of Kenya, in what is today Nandi County, and their population is nearly 1 million. They are agriculturalists and pastoralists. The Nandi speak the Nandi dialect, a Kalenjin language within the broader Nilo-Saharan linguistic family. Their documented history includes the formation of a distinct Nandi identity during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, resistance to Arab caravans and British colonial rule, and the incorporation of Nandi into the British East Africa Protectorate after the death of Koitalel Arap Samoei in 1905. Their folk-cultural profile is especially documented through territorial organization, age-sets, oral traditions, ritual leadership, warfare, and cattle-centered social life.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

They do record several historically specific forms of appearance. Members of the *korongoro* age-set were said to have gone into battle wearing *septook*, described as broken pieces of calabashes, on their ears. This was interpreted symbolically as blocking out the warning of the *Orkoiyot*, the ritual leader. During the Arab conflicts, Nandi men’s “cherished locks” were shaved by Arab traders after the defenders at Kipsoboi had been humiliated. The sources also mention Nandi shields, arrows, spears, firearms, and the use of ox-hide in the burial account of Kakipoch.

### Architecture

They do document a territorial and administrative environment organized into *emet*—counties—then *bororiet* districts and *kokwet* villages. The Nandi territory was divided into six counties by the turn of the century: Wareng, Mosop, Tindiret, Soiin, Pelkut, Aldai, Chesumei, and Emgwen are named in the account, although the description groups several names within the directional summary. The *kokwet* was an important political and judicial unit, while among the Nandi the *bororiet* was the most significant institution. These terms describe social and administrative organization rather than a documented architectural form.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Objects mentioned in historical contexts include calabashes, ox-hide, shields, bows, arrows, spears, rifles, muskets, cloth, wire, and cattle. Calabash pieces were worn by the *korongoro* age-set during the episode associated with its disappearance. Ox-hide and personal possessions appear in the account of Kakipoch’s burial, while cloth and wire were among the coastal trade goods carried by Arab caravans.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They mention *septook*, broken pieces of calabashes worn on the ears by the *korongoro* age-set in battle, and they state that Arab traders shaved the “cherished locks” of Nandi men at Kipsoboi. These references are connected with warfare and humiliation rather than a documented catalogue of adornment practices.

## Music & performance

They do identify ritual and public occasions involving collective performance or ceremonial gathering. In 1923, the *saget ab eito*, described as the sacrifice of the ox, was to transfer leadership of the community between generations. All Nandi males would gather in one place for the ceremony, which was associated with the formal recognition of a warrior age-set and an increase in cattle raiding. The ceremony was prevented from taking place after the Orkoiyot Barsirian Arap Manyei and four other elders were arrested and deported to Meru on 16 October 1923. The sources also mention the *Orkoiyot* as a ritual leader whose counsel carried authority over warriors and whose permission was sought before the Nandi attacked the Arab post at Kipsoboi.

## Dance & theatre

They do describe collective martial displays and ceremonial gatherings. The approach to the *saget ab eito* was marked by military fervour, and the ceremony brought Nandi males together in one place. The sources also describe warfare tactics in which warriors rushed toward armed opponents, dropped to the ground while muzzle-loading rifles were reloaded, and then attacked caravan porters. These accounts concern military practice rather than a documented dance or theatrical form.

## Festivals & rituals

They do document life-cycle, political, and age-based institutions. Nandi society was organized around age and gender. Males were divided into boys, warriors, and elders, while females were divided into girls and married women. The first stage began at birth and continued until initiation, which marked movement into another social role.

Boys circumcised together belonged to the same *ibinda*, or age-set. Once young men of an *ibinda* came of age, they were responsible for protecting the community and its territory. The sources state that the Kalenjin traditionally had eight cyclical age-sets, or *ibinwek*, but that the Nandi discontinued *korongoro* after its members were said to have been wiped out in war for disregarding the counsel of the *Orkoiyot*.

The *saget ab eito* was a historically significant ceremony in which leadership passed between generations. In 1923, the colonial government believed that the ceremony might be used to gather forces for a military uprising. Permission was withdrawn, and the ceremony did not take place.

## Foodways

They do mention agriculture, pastoralism, cattle, millet fields, grain shortages, and the exchange of cattle for coastal goods. During the Arab conflicts, donkeys were released to trample millet fields. In the period of stock quarantine from 1921 to 1923, Nandi people could not sell livestock outside the Reserve. The sources explain that grain shortages were normally addressed by selling stock and buying grain, but quarantine made this impossible. Cattle also had social and economic importance: returning veterans used wartime back-pay to purchase cattle, and cattle formed part of bride wealth.

## Oral tradition & literature

Nandi history is documented through oral traditions concerning settlement and identity. These traditions state that the first settlers came from Elgon during the time of the Maina and formed the *Kipoiis* clan, a name that possibly means “the spirits.” They were led by Kakipoch, who founded the Nandi section of the Kalenjin and settled in the *emet* of Aldai in south-western Nandi. His grave was said to remain marked by the stump of an ancient olive tree on Chepilat hill in Aldai. The account states that his body was placed on ox-hide with his possessions and left for the hyenas.

Other oral traditions concern the emergence of a distinct Nandi identity through the gradual joining of diverse clans, contacts in the Kipchorian/Nyando Valley, and encounters on the Uasin Gishu Plateau. The legend of the abandoned *korongoro* age-set explains its disappearance through a disastrous battle. Nandi oral tradition also remembers the hostile encounters with Arab caravans during the 1850s and the resulting “Nandi legend” that the Nandi were undefeatable.

## Language & religion

The Nandi speak the Nandi dialect, which is closely related to Kipsigis. Nandi is a Kalenjin language, and Kalenjin belongs to the broader Nilo-Saharan linguistic family. The Kalenjin dialects are broadly similar, with most described as mutually intelligible, although the dialects are also treated as distinct languages. The Nandi use Kalenjin nomenclature, and a Nandi person usually identifies themselves by personal name, family name, and place of origin.

The sources state that Kalenjin mythology was broadly similar across communities. It is thought to have developed from an earlier worship oriented toward the sky and later focused on the sun; this change may have radiated from the Kibasisek clan, originally from Marakwet. Today, most Nandi are either Protestant Christian or Catholic. The *Orkoiyot* was a ritual leader, and his authority appears in accounts of warfare, age-sets, and the 1923 political crisis.
